# Āmagandha Sutta (Snp 2.2 (PTS Snp 42))

**ID:** Snp 2.2 (PTS Snp 42)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Āmagandha Sutta* (Snp 2.2, verses 239–252) is a discourse in the *Cūḷavagga* of the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1997-2001; Winternitz 1933]. According to the commentarial tradition, the text records a dialogue originally held between the past Buddha Kassapa and the ascetic or Brahman Tissa, which Gautama Buddha subsequently recited to an ascetic named Āmagandha [Balasooriya et al. 1980; Levman 2014; Saddhatissa 2013]. The text opens with three verses wherein Tissa criticizes Kassapa for consuming fish and meat while claiming to be free from carrion or stench (*āmagandha*) [Levman 2014; Saddhatissa 2013]. In the subsequent verses, Kassapa responds by demonstrating that *āmagandha* does not denote the dietary consumption of meat (*na hi maṃsabhojanaṃ*), but rather moral defilements and unwholesome actions [Levman 2014].

The central doctrine of the sutta is that defilement is caused by unethical deeds—such as the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*), beating, mutilation, theft, lying, deceit, adultery, anger, and arrogance—rather than the eating of flesh [Balasooriya et al. 1980; Omvedt 2003; Winternitz 1933]. The refrain *esāmagandho na hi maṃsabhojanaṃ* ("this is tainted fare, not the eating of flesh") drives home this transvaluation of Brahmanical ritual purity into ethical purity [Balasooriya et al. 1980; Levman 2014]. Furthermore, verse 249 emphasizes that external ascetic observances, vegetarianism, and rituals cannot purify a person who has not overcome spiritual doubt [Balasooriya et al. 1980].

Saddhatissa under the title *Stench* [Saddhatissa 2013].
